newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-U.S. Q1 labor costs seen modestly higher.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-U.S. Q1 labor costs seen modestly higher.

text.p: Modest increases in U.S. benefits costs helped U.S. employers offset growing wage pressures in the first quarter, but that could be the last good news on employment costs for a while, analysts said.

The quarterly Employment Cost Index (ECI), set for release next Tuesday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, grew about 0.9 percent in the first three months of 1997, economists estimated. That compares with a 0.8 percent rise in fourth-quarter 1996.
"We might see a slight edging up of benefits and wages, but nothing dramatic," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.
As in previous ECI reports, benefits costs should show slower growth than wages and salaries, mostly because of more restrained increases in healthcare costs, economists said.
But the healthcare trend may have run its course, the experts said.
Cost advantages that firms enjoyed from higher deductibles, reduced coverage or the switch to managed care providers cannot continue indefinitely, they said.

"Now, you're starting to see surveys suggesting people expect healthcare costs to increase more going forward than they have in the past," said Pierre Ellis, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics.
"If that's in fact the case, then it's definitely going to be reflected in this benefit cost piece. And it's not going to help overall compensation anymore," he said.
Benefits costs grew 0.7 percent in the last quarter of 1996 but only 2.0 percent for the entire year. Estimates for 1997 put annual benefits costs up about 3.0 to 3.5 percent.
"I think we will start to see benefits costs going up rapidly, and I would expect that to actually begin in this report," Norwest's Sohn said.
That forecast remains uncertain, though, since some economists wonder if other, longer-term efficiences could develop within the medical care industry.
"This is a big question, for the (Federal Reserve) in particular," Ellis said.
In his February Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before the Senate Banking Committee, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan mentioned the difficulty of estimating health services-related price growth.
Of course, wage and salary costs remain a top concern of the Fed as well, and they appear likely to show another solid rise for the first quarter.
"We expect job growth to continue to be fairly strong and therefore wage rates to remain under upward pressure," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.
Monthly employment reports showed moderate wage gains in early 1997, and the wages and salaries component of the ECI should fall roughly in line.
Like benefits costs, wage outlays are not forecast to ease anytime soon. Labor force growth cannot keep up with the demand for workers, economists said.
Sohn said workforce expansion statistics might be somewhat misleading. Wage increases have persuaded discouraged workers and older workers to seek jobs, he said.
But many firms need workers with more skills than those who are returning to the labor pool, Sohn said.

"Because presumably all the high-quality workers have already been hired, we are really getting down to more marginal workers," he said. "Labor capacity will be a drawback, and that has to mean acceleration of wages."
The key question, however, is whether the projected higher compensation costs will begin showing up in consumer prices. Most economists said that eventually, they will.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1868))
